title: Designing a Chess Game
description: Model chess pieces using inheritance, validate moves with strategy patterns, represent the board efficiently, and detect check and checkmate.

segments.text: Chess is the ultimate object-oriented design playground. Every piece has unique movement rules, yet they all share common behavior. Let's model this elegantly.
First, the board. An eight-by-eight grid. Each cell holds either a piece or null. We represent it as a two-dimensional array of Cell objects, each with a row, column, and optional piece reference.
Now the pieces. An abstract Piece class with color and position. Six subclasses: King, Queen, Rook, Bishop, Knight, and Pawn. Each overrides a canMove method with its own movement logic.
The Rook moves in straight lines. The Bishop moves diagonally. The Queen combines both. The Knight jumps in an L-shape. Each piece validates its own move geometry independently.
But geometry alone is not enough. A move must also check: is the path clear? Is the destination occupied by a friendly piece? Would this move leave your own king in check? Three layers of validation.
Here is something to think about.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you detect if the king is in check? What data structures would make this efficient?

segments.text: To detect check, iterate over all opponent pieces and see if any can legally move to the king's square. If yes, the king is in check. Store piece positions in a set for constant-time lookup.
Checkmate means the king is in check AND has no legal move to escape. No square the king can move to is safe, no piece can block the attack, and no piece can capture the attacker.

Do not forget special moves. Castling requires neither the king nor rook has moved, no pieces between them, and the king does not pass through check. En passant and pawn promotion add more edge cases.

The Game class orchestrates everything. It tracks whose turn it is, maintains move history for undo support, and checks end conditions: checkmate, stalemate, draw by repetition, or the fifty-move rule.

segments.thought_prompt: What design pattern would you use to handle the undo/redo of moves?

segments.text: The Command pattern captures each move as an object with execute and undo methods. Chess teaches you inheritance hierarchies, validation pipelines, and game state management. These patterns transfer directly to workflow engines and rule-based systems.
